title: Your cache key is a specification
thesis: A cache key enumerates everything the render depends on, so getting it wrong is a correctness bug rather than a performance one.
body:
We put a read-through cache in front of the render pipeline in March, and p99 on the article pages fell from 810ms to 120ms — measured over the seven days either side of the change, on warm cache. That number is the reason anyone would read this. The rest of it is the reason I would not repeat the week that followed.

## Why it was slow, and why a cache was even possible

Every request re-rendered the whole document tree, including the parts nobody had touched since the last publish. Profiling put 78% of wall time inside the Markdown-to-AST step. That step is deterministic for a given input, which is the only reason a cache was on the table at all: if the same input can render differently, a cache is not a latency win, it is a staleness generator with a hit rate.

## The key that named two of its three inputs

The first version keyed on the document path:

```python
def cache_key(request):
    return request.path
```

Two things fell out of that within the week. Readers on a non-default locale were served the English render, because locale was an input to the render and not to the key. And an error page rendered during a deploy was cached and served for forty minutes, because status was an input to whether the response should be cached at all.

Neither of those is a caching bug in the usual sense. Nothing expired late; nothing was evicted early. The key simply did not name everything the render depended on, and a cache key that under-names its inputs is not a performance shortcut with a bug in it — it is a wrong answer, served fast.

## What I would do differently

I think the real mistake was treating invalidation as the task after the cache rather than as part of its design. Writing the key first, as a list of everything the render reads, would have caught both bugs before either shipped.

Write the key as a specification of the render's inputs, and invalidation stops being a separate task you get to later.
